extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and students of natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive chapter-level criteria and observations about secondary sexual characters and behaviours in insects (and comparisons with other arthropods), used to infer sexual selection mechanisms such as female choice, male-male competition, ornaments, and acoustic signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturation-linked acquisition of sexual ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Males often do not acquire conspicuous colours or other sexual characters until they become mature and nearly ready to breed; this timing is characteristic of traits produced by sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: male Gelasimus acquires bright colours only upon maturity; male sand-hopper Orchestia acquires large claspers only when nearly full grown. This developmental timing is presented as strong evidence that such characters evolved via sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing sexual selection from ecological/habitual causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in colour or form between sexes may sometimes be due to differing habits or exposures (e.g., males wandering more and being more exposed to light) rather than sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution before attributing dimorphism to sexual selection; consider alternative explanations such as habitat, behaviour, or wear (Mr. Bate's remarks; Dr. Power's unsuccessful attempts to distinguish sexes by colour except in special cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-specific ornamental or colour-producing organs as potential sexual signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of male-specific colour-producing structures (e.g., minute shields or cell-like bodies showing changing colours) may indicate ornaments used in attracting females, but this inference can be tenuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Saphirina males have cell-like bodies with changing colours absent in females. Author warns it would be 'extremely rash' to conclude such organs serve to attract females without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male behavioral courtship and female choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of male courtship behaviour and female acceptance or rejection (hesitation, threats, selective acceptance) constitute evidence for female choice shaping male traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: spiders where females threaten and sometimes reject courting males (Canestrini); crickets and other insects where males display and females respond. Such accounts are used to infer that female preference can drive the evolution of male ornaments or behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male-male competition and combat-related structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures that enable males to compete with each other (horns, enlarged mandibles, jaws) or behaviours of pugnacity imply sexual selection via male-male competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: horns in some Diptera (Elaphomyia), great mandibles in Corydalis cornutus and stag-beetles (Lucanus), battles observed in many groups. Where males fight for females, selection favors size/weaponry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures for seizing and holding females
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous modified appendages (claspers, prehensile hooks, membranous suckers, dilated tarsi, specialized tail appendages) function to grasp or secure the female during mating and are part of sexual adaptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: modified legs in Diplopoda, tarsal suckers in male water-beetles, dragon-fly tail appendages modified to embrace female neck. Such structures may be classed near primary organs but are functionally important in mating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual differences in size and developmental timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Males commonly smaller than females in insects, often maturing earlier than females; exceptions occur (males larger) when size confers advantage for fighting or transporting females (marriage flights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace's hypothesis: earlier maturation of smaller males ensures many males ready when females emerge. Exceptions: large males in stag-beetles, certain bees and fossorial wasps when strength/size is necessary for mating behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic signalling by males as sexual calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Males of several insect orders produce sounds (stridulation, drumming, humming) that serve to call, excite, or attract mute females and to mediate male rivalry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cicadidae loud daytime songs attracting females; Orthoptera (crickets, locusts, grasshoppers) with specialised stridulatory organs; Diptera humming during courtship; observations of females approaching drumming males. Rivalry and female attraction often both involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical specialisation of sound-producing organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different insect families have distinct mechanical structures for producing sound (e.g., toothed nervures scraped across a hard nervure in Achetidae; asymmetric bow-and-fiddle wing-covers and speculum in Locustidae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed examples: Gryllus teeth and r ridge; Chlorocoelus wing-lobes; variation in apparatus specialization correlates with performance (Locustidae more specialized than Achetidae). Development via selection and mechanical stimulation noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in sensory structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexes may differ in sensory organs (e.g., pectinate antennae in males, pillared eyes in male Chloeon) that enhance male ability to locate or court females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: males with more elaborate antennae or eyes, ocelli absent in some females; such differences may be adaptive for detecting females or their signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female morphological modifications facilitating mating
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, morphological features of females (grooved elytra, hairy surfaces, punctured elytra) appear adapted to assist the male in holding on during copulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: female Dytiscus with grooved elytra, Acilius sulcatus with hairs, Hydroporus punctured elytra. These traits suggest co-adaptation of female morphology to male grasping structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning coloration and mimicry can confound sexual explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous colours or luminescence may function as aposematic signals (warning of unpalatability) or be mimicked by others, rather than for sexual attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lampyridae (glow-worms) are distasteful and luminous; Bates and Belt suggest luminosity may signal unpalatability and be mimicked—therefore brightness may not always indicate sexual signalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and polymorphism in male sexual traits as indicator of recent or ongoing selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme variability in male traits (colour, form) or presence of two male morphs suggests sexual characters not yet fixed and indicates ongoing selection dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Theridion lineatum male colour variability; Canestrini's report of two male forms with different jaw sizes. Such variability is taken as evidence that sexual traits can be in flux under selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution that many sexual differences have unknown function
rubrics_metrics.description: The sexes of many species present differences 'of which the meaning is not understood'; not all dimorphisms have clear adaptive explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: beetle with greatly enlarged left mandible distorting mouth; species where the female head is broader than the male. Author acknowledges many cases defy current interpretation and should not be over-interpreted.
